Use the two journeys to connect mechanisms from [the lecture](lec.qmd). Draw the

The [quiz](quiz.qmd) gives a shorter self-check.

## G-level questions

**1.** Follow an mRNA–LNP from a particle outside a cell to productive translation.
Name the two membrane barriers, explain endocytosis and escape, and distinguish
the paths of the lipid carrier, mRNA and encoded protein.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
The plasma membrane separates extracellular space from cytosol. **Endocytosis**
encloses the particle in an intracellular vesicle, so the cargo crosses the cell
boundary without being released into cytosol. The **endosomal membrane** is a
second barrier: intact mRNA must become accessible to cytosolic ribosomes before
it is degraded. Ionisable carrier lipids can favour membrane interactions during
acidification; the exact escape route depends on formulation and cell type.
The **lipids** can traffic or be metabolised separately, the **mRNA** is translated
in the cytoplasm and eventually degraded, and the **protein** follows its own
sequence-dependent targeting route. Neither carrier uptake nor persistent lipid
fluorescence demonstrates cytosolic delivery of functional mRNA.
:::

---

**2.** A delivered mRNA encodes a protein with a cleavable ER signal peptide, a
large antigen domain and a membrane anchor. Explain how the antigen domain
reaches the ER lumen and what can happen if it fails to fold. Why must you inspect
the remaining sequence before predicting the effect of deleting the signal peptide?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Translation begins on a cytosolic ribosome. **SRP** recognises the emerging signal,
directs the ribosome to the ER, and translation feeds the chain through a
**translocon**. The signal is cleaved; the antigen domain enters the lumen, where
chaperones help it fold and N-glycans can be added. Its membrane anchor retains
it in the bilayer. Failed folding causes retention and can lead to **ER-associated
degradation**: export to cytosol, ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
Deleting a cleavable signal does not necessarily prevent all ER targeting:
a remaining hydrophobic segment may act as an **internal signal-anchor**, possibly
with altered topology. A simple “cytosolic protein” prediction requires the
assumption that no functional alternative targeting signal remains.
:::

---

**3.** Trace a correctly folded membrane antigen from ER to cell surface. Mark
which side contains its glycosylated antigen domain and which contains its
cytosolic tail at each stage. Give a way to test the final orientation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
ER → transport carriers → Golgi → carriers from the trans-Golgi network → plasma
membrane. The antigen domain faces the **lumen** of each compartment; the tail
faces the **cytosol**. Fusion with the plasma membrane exposes the carrier lumen
to the outside, placing antigen and glycans **extracellularly**. Test with
antibodies against the external domain and cytosolic tail: in intact viable,
non-permeabilised cells only the external epitope is accessible. Permeabilisation
allows both to be detected. Include antibody-specificity and membrane-integrity
controls. A total-protein measurement alone cannot establish surface orientation.
:::

---

**4.** Explain how cytoskeletal transport and organelle homeostasis support the
journey. Give two reasons a global ATP-depletion experiment cannot isolate a
single failed step.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Microtubules and motors position organelles and move many carriers; actin and
myosins contribute to local traffic. Motor transport works with docking and
fusion machinery rather than replacing it. Energy supports translation, chaperone
cycles and motor activity. ATP-driven pumps establish organelle pH and calcium
conditions, so mitochondria and glycolysis support several steps indirectly.
ATP depletion can therefore impair **both protein production and trafficking**,
while also disrupting compartment chemistry or damaging cells. A reduced surface
signal does not distinguish these effects. Use a time course, viability controls
and more focused perturbations, measuring the earliest affected event.
:::

---

**5.** Compare whole-antigen display with classical peptide–MHC-I display. Which
route uses secretory transport, and which uses the proteasome? Why does neither
measurement alone establish a complete immune response?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
A whole membrane antigen folds and reaches the surface through **ER and Golgi
traffic**. In the classical MHC-I route, the **proteasome** generates peptides;
peptides are transported into the ER, loaded onto MHC-I, and peptide–MHC-I complexes
also pass through the secretory pathway to the surface. Thus secretory transport
contributes to both, while proteolysis is central to peptide generation. Folded
antigen and peptide–MHC engage different immune receptors. Immune responses also
depend on the presenting cell, receptor specificity, costimulation, cytokines
and other interactions. Antigen production in one cell is evidence of expression,
not proof of immune protection. Other presentation routes are covered in Immunologi.
:::

---

**6.** Follow imatinib from outside a leukaemia cell to inhibition of BCR–ABL1.
Explain why total cellular drug, target engagement and downstream phosphorylation
are different measurements.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Available extracellular drug enters the cell; entry, export, binding and
sequestration determine the amount accessible at the target. Imatinib binds the
BCR–ABL1 kinase domain and reduces its signalling. **Total cellular drug** includes
bound or sequestered material and does not automatically give free target-site
concentration. **Target engagement** tests interaction with the intended protein.
**Phosphorylation** reports kinase or pathway action, which may change indirectly.
A validated target-dependent readout, total-protein controls and an appropriate
time course help connect the measurements. This route acts on an existing protein
and does not require translation of a new therapeutic protein or Golgi export.
:::

---

**7.** Explain how kinase inhibition can cause cell-cycle arrest or intrinsic
apoptosis. Which measurements distinguish those outcomes, and why is a smaller
cell population insufficient evidence of death?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Reduced mitogenic signalling can lower cyclin/CDK activity and prevent cell-cycle
progression. Reduced survival signalling can shift BCL-2-family control towards
BAX/BAK activation, mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilisation, cytochrome c
release and caspase activation. The outcome depends on cellular dependencies
and the state of the death machinery. Measure **DNA synthesis or cell-cycle
profiles** for proliferation and **caspase activation with complementary viability
or membrane-integrity measurements** for death. Compare time courses and controls.
A population can become smaller relative to control simply because it divides
more slowly; this does not require cells to die.
:::

---

**8.** Compare three resistance mechanisms: increased drug efflux, a resistant
kinase and a downstream survival bypass. Predict whether each can preserve growth
and whether it must prevent inhibition of the intended kinase.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
**Increased efflux** can lower target-site exposure so kinase activity remains
sufficient. **Target resistance**, such as a mutation reducing imatinib sensitivity,
can preserve kinase activity despite adequate exposure. **A downstream bypass**
can sustain growth or survival even when the intended kinase is inhibited.
All can reduce treatment response, but only the third explicitly allows intact
target inhibition with continued downstream function. Test exposure, target
sequence/abundance and target action before assigning the mechanism; pathways
can change together. Clinical resistance is not diagnosed from a cell count alone.
:::

## VG-level questions

**9. [VG]** Two mRNA formulations give the following results in equal numbers of
viable cells at the same time. Values are normalised to formulation A. Interpret
the difference and design two measurements to distinguish competing explanations.

| Readout | A | B |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cell-associated lipid fluorescence | 100 | 180 |
| Total encoded protein | 100 | 25 |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
B has **more cell-associated lipid label but less protein expression**. It does
not follow that B delivered more intact mRNA to cytosol. Possibilities include
more surface-bound or endosomally trapped carrier, separation of lipid and RNA,
RNA degradation, or impaired translation. Measure (1) cargo location and cytosolic
access, for example using a validated access reporter with membrane-damage
controls, and (2) intact RNA and/or translation competence with an independent
control mRNA delivered by another method. Surface-label removal or quenching and
endosomal colocalisation can distinguish some uptake artefacts. Viability
normalisation does not exclude sublethal stress. The table alone cannot uniquely
locate the defect or establish which formulation would work better in vivo.
:::

---

**10. [VG]** After a treatment, total antigen remains near control but surface
antigen falls sharply. RNA delivery is unchanged. Compare an ER-folding defect
with an ER-to-Golgi traffic block. Design a test that distinguishes them, including
a control and a limitation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Both can lower surface delivery while leaving initial translation intact.
A **folding defect** can retain antigen in the ER and eventually send it to ERAD;
a **traffic block** can retain folded cargo before Golgi arrival. Use a time-resolved
pulse-chase or equivalent synthesis/chase experiment, combined with ER/Golgi
localisation and a folding- or conformation-sensitive assay. Include an unrelated
secretory cargo: a general transport block should affect that cargo too, whereas
a cargo-specific folding mutation may not. Endo-H sensitivity can support failure
to acquire Golgi processing but cannot alone distinguish the two hypotheses,
because both ER-retained proteins may remain sensitive. Check synthesis,
membrane integrity and viability. Imaging localisation without a folding test
cannot establish whether the retained cargo is correctly folded.
:::

---

**11. [VG]** Three leukaemia cell lines receive the same extracellular inhibitor.
A validated target-dependent phosphorylation readout and DNA synthesis are measured
relative to vehicle controls. Propose a next test for each line. Do not assign a
unique molecular mechanism from the table.

| Line | Target-dependent phosphorylation | DNA synthesis |
|---|---:|---:|
| X | 15 % | 20 % |
| Y | 95 % | 95 % |
| Z | 15 % | 90 % |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
**X:** pathway action and DNA synthesis both fall, consistent with target-dependent
proliferation. Measure cell-cycle distribution and apoptosis separately to
distinguish arrest from death. **Y:** little pathway inhibition; measure cellular
exposure and target engagement, then test target sequence/abundance. Low exposure
and a resistant or abundant target are alternatives, not conclusions. **Z:** the
intended pathway readout falls while DNA synthesis persists; investigate alternative
growth signalling, incomplete duration of inhibition or assay timing. Test a
candidate bypass by an independent perturbation rather than merely correlating
its expression. Use matched time courses, replicate wells, total-protein controls
and viable-cell counts. Neither DNA synthesis nor phosphorylation alone establishes
long-term response or clinical efficacy.
:::

## Explore {#explore}

**Demo: drug journey.** Choose **mRNA–LNP** or **Imatinib** and use **Next** and
**Previous**, or select a numbered stop. The map follows a mechanism one event at
a time; it has no automatic biological clock. The endpoint readouts are
**qualitative predictions**, not measured data or probabilities of treatment success.
Choose a **What-if** scenario only after making your own prediction. Switching
journeys returns to its first stop and Baseline; changing a scenario keeps the
current stop so you can compare it directly.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="drugjourney"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/drugjourney.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Select **mRNA–LNP**, Baseline. Step through all seven stops. At **Escape**,
**Translation**, **ER/Golgi** and **Surface/peptides**, name the molecule being
followed and which side of a membrane it occupies. Does the mRNA pass through
the Golgi?

**E2.** Predict, then select **Impaired endosomal escape**. Which readouts could
still look successful even though protein expression falls? Why would increasing
particle fluorescence not resolve the problem?

**E3. [VG]** Compare **No ER-targeting signal** with **Secretory traffic block**.
Which early events can remain intact? Why must the signal scenario assume that
no alternative signal-anchor redirects the protein? Does failed whole-antigen
surface display necessarily eliminate every antigen-derived peptide?

**E4.** Switch to **Imatinib** and follow the five stops. Compare **Increased drug
efflux** and **Resistant target**. Which measurement helps distinguish the two
assumptions, and which would show whether kinase activity actually fell?

**E5. [VG]** The kinase readout falls but cells remain alive. Explain why this
need not contradict the drug's molecular mechanism. Choose separate tests for
cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis and a survival bypass, then explain what the map
cannot decide for you.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** Escape moves intact **mRNA from endosomal lumen to cytosol**, where
ribosomes can translate it. Translation starts in cytosol. The emerging protein's
ER signal directs the growing chain into/along the ER membrane; the antigen domain
faces the **ER lumen**. The protein travels through Golgi and secretory carriers
to the surface, where that domain faces **outside**. Peptide–MHC display is a
separate processing route. The mRNA and LNP do not need to travel through the
Golgi with the antigen.

**E2.** Particle association and uptake can remain high, while cytosolic access
and expression are low. A fluorescent lipid reports its own location, not
necessarily that of intact mRNA. Measure cargo integrity and cytosolic access,
with endosomal, membrane-damage and viability controls.

**E3.** Both scenarios can preserve uptake, escape and initial translation.
In the signal scenario, ER targeting is assumed to fail; in the traffic scenario,
protein can enter the ER but fail to reach its later destination. Real sequences
can contain internal signal-anchors, so deleting a signal peptide is not a
universal way to prevent ER entry. A protein that fails to appear intact at the
surface can still provide **proteasomal peptides**, depending on its synthesis,
degradation and the cell's presentation machinery. The simple map cannot predict
the full set of peptide–MHC complexes or an immune response.

**E4.** Increased efflux assumes lower drug available at the target; target
resistance assumes reduced inhibitor sensitivity. Compare exposure and target
engagement, sequence/abundance and a validated kinase-action readout. Similar
endpoint growth patterns do not distinguish the causes. The scenario selector
chooses a mechanism for illustration; it has not diagnosed one from data.

**E5.** Cells can arrest without immediately dying, persist through alternative
survival routes, or respond on a different timescale. Assess DNA synthesis and
cell-cycle profiles for arrest, caspase activation plus complementary viability
measures for apoptosis, and controlled perturbation of a candidate pathway for
a bypass. The map supplies a causal story and predictions; it does not model
cell-state diversity, actual drug concentrations or clinical response.
:::

## Selected primary sources

- [Gilleron et al., 2013](https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2612): imaging of LNP-delivered
  **siRNA** uptake, trafficking and escape; used here for the distinction between
  uptake and productive delivery, not as a numerical vaccine model.
- [Pardi et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4624045/): expression
  kinetics of LNP-delivered modified mRNA in mice; reporter expression is a
  different measurement from particle uptake.
- [Druker et al., 2001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11287972/): early clinical
  evidence for inhibiting BCR–ABL in CML.
- [Gorre et al., 2001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11423618/): target mutation
  or amplification associated with imatinib resistance in the studied samples.
